ai.title: Tinea Pedis (Athlete's Foot)
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A superficial dermatophyte infection of the feet, most often caused by *Trichophyton rubrum*. It presents with pruritic, scaling, and fissuring between toes and on the sole. Prompt diagnosis and antifungal therapy prevent spread and complications.

b: Common in athletes, people in communal showers, and those with poorly ventilated footwear.
sections.p: Tinea pedis is a common superficial fungal infection of the skin of the feet, especially the interdigital spaces. It is caused by dermatophytes that thrive in warm, moist environments.

b: Hyphae produce keratinases; spores are resistant to desiccation.
sections.p: The principal pathogen is *Trichophyton rubrum*, a keratinophilic dermatophyte that grows on keratinized skin.

b: Human-to-human spread is uncommon; indirect spread dominates.
sections.p: Infection occurs by direct contact with contaminated surfaces or via fomites. The fungus survives on shoes, mats, and in communal showers for months.

b: Severity ranges from mild maceration to extensive fissuring and secondary bacterial infection.
sections.p: Tinea pedis manifests as pruritus, erythema, scaling, fissuring, and sometimes blistering between toes and on the sole.

b: If culture unavailable, treat empirically based on clinical picture.
sections.p: Clinical examination is usually sufficient. Confirmatory tests are reserved for atypical or recalcitrant cases.

sections.p: First‑line therapy is topical azoles; systemic therapy is reserved for extensive or refractory disease.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, clinical diagnosis is key. Look for classic interdigital scaling and fissures. Treat early to prevent secondary bacterial infection and spread to nails.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain, spreading cellulitis, fever, or signs of systemic infection.
